symptom_text: Bacterial leaf spot of tomato causes small, water-soaked, greasy-appearing circular to irregular lesions on leaves that rapidly enlarge and turn brown to black with a yellow halo surrounding the necrotic tissue. Lesions are typically 3–5 mm in diameter, angular and constrained by leaf veins, with a dark brown to black center that may dry out and fall away giving a shot-hole appearance. Spots are distributed across the leaf blade and are most numerous on older, lower leaves first, though the disease progresses upward. Severely infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely. Similar dark, raised, scab-like lesions with water-soaked margins can also appear on fruit, stems, and petioles.

pathogen.value: Xanthomonas vesicatoria, X. euvesicatoria, X. gardneri, X. perforans
pathogen.verbatim_quote: Bacterial spot of tomato and pepper is caused by four species of Xanthomonas: X. euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, and X. gardneri.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Bacterial spot can affect all above-ground parts of a tomato plant, including the leaves, stems, and fruit.

visual_symptoms.value: Small water-soaked lesions that turn dark brown to black, often with yellow halos; lesions may coalesce; fruit develops raised, scab-like spots with water-soaked margins
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: On leaves, bacterial spot first appears as small, water-soaked, circular to irregular spots. The spots turn brown to black, and are often surrounded by a yellow halo. Severely infected leaves turn yellow and drop from the plant. On fruit, the disease first appears as small, raised, water-soaked spots that later become brown and scab-like.

symptom_text: Early blight on tomato manifests as dark brown to black, circular to angular lesions primarily on older, lower leaves, with each lesion displaying distinctive concentric rings forming a characteristic target-board or bull's-eye pattern. Lesions are typically surrounded by a yellow chlorotic halo and may coalesce under heavy disease pressure, causing extensive blighting and defoliation. The necrotic tissue within lesions often appears dry and papery in texture. Similar lesions can also develop on stems, petioles, and fruit, particularly near the stem end, where dark, sunken, leathery spots with concentric rings may form.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Early blight can affect leaves, stems, and fruit of tomatoes.

visual_symptoms.value: Dark brown to black circular lesions with concentric rings (target-board pattern) surrounded by yellow halos on lower leaves; sunken dark lesions with concentric rings on fruit near stem end
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Symptoms first appear on the older, lower leaves as small, brown spots with concentric rings that form a target-board effect. Spots are surrounded by a yellow halo. As the disease progresses, the entire leaf may turn yellow and drop.

symptom_text: Gray mold on tomato, caused by Botrytis cinerea, produces water-soaked, tan to brown lesions on leaves, stems, blossoms, and fruit that rapidly expand and become covered with a characteristic gray, powdery to fuzzy sporulating mass of conidia. On stems, the pathogen causes girdling cankers that are pale brown and may cause wilting of the shoot above the infection site. Infected blossoms turn brown and collapse, and fruit develop firm, brown, leathery rot often beginning at the calyx end or at wounds; under humid conditions the entire affected surface becomes blanketed with the dense gray sporulation that gives the disease its name.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Gray mold, caused by Botrytis cinerea, is one of the most common and economically important diseases of tomato worldwide.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Gray mold can affect all above-ground parts of the tomato plant including leaves, stems, flowers, and fruit.

visual_symptoms.value: Water-soaked lesions turning tan to brown, covered with gray fuzzy sporulation; stem cankers; blighted blossoms; brown fruit rot at calyx end
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Infected tissue initially appears water-soaked and then turns tan to brown. Under moist conditions, a gray, fuzzy mass of spores (conidia) develops on the surface of infected tissue, giving the disease its common name.

symptom_text: Tomato late blight presents as large, irregularly shaped, water-soaked lesions on leaves that rapidly turn brown to dark brown or olive-green, often with a greasy or oily appearance, and are frequently bordered by a pale yellow-green halo; under humid conditions, a white cottony or downy sporulating growth of the pathogen appears on the undersides of leaves at lesion margins. Stems develop dark brown to black firm lesions that can girdle and collapse the plant. Fruit infections appear as large, firm, brown, greasy-looking lesions typically starting at the shoulders, often with a rough or corrugated surface texture, and the affected tissue remains firm unlike bacterial rots.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Late blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Late blight can affect all above ground parts of tomato plants including leaves, stems, and fruit.

visual_symptoms.value: Large, irregularly shaped, water-soaked, brown to dark brown lesions on leaves with white sporulation on undersides; dark brown to black stem lesions; firm, brown, greasy lesions on fruit
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Leaf symptoms begin as small, water-soaked lesions that are often pale green to yellow. These lesions enlarge rapidly and turn brown to dark brown. Under humid conditions, a white, cottony growth (sporangia and sporangiophores) may be visible on the underside of leaves at the margin of lesions. On fruit, late blight causes large, firm, brown, greasy-looking lesions, often starting at the shoulders of the fruit.

symptom_text: Tomato leaf mold presents primarily on leaves, beginning as pale greenish-yellow to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface that are irregular to diffuse in shape. On the corresponding lower leaf surface, a distinctive olive-green to grayish-purple velvety or powdery fungal sporulation develops beneath these chlorotic areas. As the disease progresses, affected leaves may curl, wither, and drop prematurely, with lesions coalescing to cover large portions of the leaf blade. Symptoms typically appear first on older, lower leaves and advance upward through the canopy under conditions of high humidity.

pathogen.value: Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva / Cladosporium fulvum)
pathogen.verbatim_quote: Leaf mold of tomato is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (previously known as Fulvia fulva or Cladosporium fulvum).

affected_organs.value: Leaves (primarily); occasionally petioles, blossoms, and fruit
affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Leaf mold primarily affects the foliage of tomato, but under severe conditions, blossoms and fruit can also be infected.

visual_symptoms.value: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surface with olive-green to grayish-purple velvety sporulation on the lower leaf surface
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Pale green to yellow spots form on the upper surface of leaves. On the lower leaf surface, olive-green to grayish-purple velvety sporulation (spores and fruiting structures of the fungus) develops beneath these spots.

symptom_text: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) causes a distinctive mottled appearance on leaves, characterized by irregular patches of light green, yellow, and dark green intermingled across the leaf blade, creating a mosaic-like pattern. Affected leaflets may display distortion, puckering, and downward curling, with the lamina often appearing blistered or rugose in texture. Symptoms are distributed throughout the plant but are most pronounced on young, actively growing leaves. In severe infections, leaflets may become narrow and fern-like (a condition called 'fernleaf'), and overall plant stunting is common. Fruits on infected plants can show internal browning and uneven ripening.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a member of the genus Tobamovirus in the family Virgaviridae.

Phytophthora blight on tomato, caused by Phytophthora infestans, produces large, irregularly shaped, water-soaked lesions that rapidly turn brown to dark brown or black on leaves, stems, and fruit. Leaf lesions often appear greasy or oily at first, then expand quickly to encompass entire leaflets, which collapse and die. A white, cottony sporulation (sporangiophores and sporangia) may be visible on the underside of infected leaves under humid conditions. Stem lesions appear as dark brown to black, girdling cankers that cause wilting and collapse of the plant above the infection point. On fruit, firm, brown, greasy-looking lesions develop, often covering large portions of the surface, sometimes with white sporulation visible at the lesion margins. Disease spread is rapid under cool, wet conditions and can devastate entire plantings.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Late blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans.

affected_organs.verbatim_quote: Late blight can affect all above ground parts of tomato plants including leaves, stems, and fruit.

visual_symptoms.value: Water-soaked, irregularly shaped lesions that turn brown to black on leaves and stems; white sporulation on leaf undersides under humid conditions; firm, brown, greasy lesions on fruit
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: Leaf lesions are large, irregularly shaped, and appear water-soaked or greasy. Lesions turn brown to black. White sporulation may be visible on the underside of leaves. Stem lesions are dark brown to black. Fruit lesions are firm, brown, and greasy-looking.

symptom_text: Tomato powdery mildew appears primarily on leaves as circular to irregular white or pale-gray powdery fungal colonies on the upper leaf surface, occasionally extending to the lower surface and stems. Early infections produce small, discrete white powdery spots that coalesce into larger patches covering much of the leaf blade. Affected leaves may yellow and curl, and severely infected foliage can dry out and drop prematurely. The powdery coating consists of fungal mycelium and conidia visible to the naked eye, giving leaves a dusty, flour-dusted appearance. Lesions typically begin on older, lower leaves and progress upward through the canopy.

pathogen.value: Leveillula taurica (anamorph: Oidiopsis sicula) and Oidium neolycopersici

visual_symptoms.value: White powdery spots or patches on upper and lower leaf surfaces; yellowing and premature leaf drop

symptom_text: Septoria leaf spot on tomato, caused by Septoria lycopersici, primarily affects the leaves, beginning on the oldest, lowest leaves and progressing upward. Lesions are small, circular to angular, roughly 3–5 mm in diameter, with dark brown to black margins and tan to gray or white centers. Within the pale centers, tiny dark brown to black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) are visible, often appearing as raised dots. Severely infected leaves turn yellow, then brown, and eventually wither and drop, leading to progressive defoliation from the base of the plant upward. Stems and calyx may also be affected in severe cases.

Southern blight on tomato is characterized by a rapid wilting and collapse of the entire plant, beginning with yellowing and browning of lower leaves. A white, cottony mycelial mat fans out across the soil surface and up the stem at or just below the soil line, often extending several centimeters in all directions. Embedded within this mycelium are small, round sclerotia that initially appear white and then turn tan to dark brown, resembling mustard seeds in size and shape. The stem at the soil line develops a water-soaked, brown to reddish-brown lesion that girdles the plant, causing the cortical tissue to rot and the plant to collapse. The disease is most conspicuous at the crown and basal stem, with the characteristic white mycelial fan and sclerotia being the definitive diagnostic features.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Southern blight is caused by Sclerotium rolfsii Sacc. (teleomorph: Athelia rolfsii (Curzi) Tu & Kimbrough)

visual_symptoms.value: White mycelial mat at soil line with tan to brown sclerotia; water-soaked stem lesion causing plant wilt and collapse
visual_symptoms.verbatim_quote: The most diagnostic feature of southern blight is the white mycelial mat that develops on the soil surface and lower stem, along with the presence of sclerotia that are initially white and turn tan to dark brown at maturity, resembling mustard seeds.

symptom_text: Spider mite infestations on tomato plants produce distinctive stippling damage primarily on leaves, where tiny, pale yellow or white flecks appear across the upper leaf surface as the mites pierce individual plant cells and extract their contents. As feeding intensifies, affected leaves take on a bronzed, silvery, or bleached appearance and may curl, dry out, and drop prematurely. Fine silken webbing — a hallmark sign of heavy infestation — is visible on the undersides of leaves and between stems and foliage. Damage typically begins on older, lower leaves and progresses upward through the canopy, with the undersides of leaves harboring dense colonies of tiny, eight-legged mites visible under magnification.

Target spot on tomato, caused by Corynespora cassiicola, produces circular to irregular brown lesions on leaves that display distinctive concentric rings resembling a target or bull's-eye pattern, often surrounded by a yellow halo; lesions typically begin as small, water-soaked spots that enlarge and develop dark brown centers with lighter brown outer rings. On stems, elongated brown lesions may appear, while fruit infections produce slightly sunken, dark brown, circular spots. Severe infections cause extensive leaf yellowing and defoliation, with lesions distributed across lower and upper leaf surfaces throughout the canopy.

Tomato leaf mould, caused by the fungal pathogen Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva / Cladosporium fulvum), primarily affects the leaves of tomato plants. On the upper leaf surface, pale greenish-yellow to yellow spots or patches appear, often with diffuse, irregular margins. On the corresponding lower leaf surface, these spots are covered by a distinctive olive-green to grayish-brown velvety or powdery sporulation (conidiophores and conidia), which is the hallmark sign of the disease. Infected leaves may curl, wither, and drop prematurely as lesions coalesce. Lower, older leaves are typically affected first, with the disease progressing upward through the canopy under conditions of high humidity.

pathogen.value: Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva, Cladosporium fulvum)

Tomato plants infected with Verticillium wilt exhibit yellowing that typically begins on the lower, older leaves and progresses upward, often appearing first on one side of the leaf or plant, giving a characteristic asymmetrical or V-shaped yellow lesion on the leaf blade. Affected leaflets develop interveinal chlorosis and necrosis, eventually wilting and dying while remaining attached to the stem. A diagnostic brown to tan discoloration of the vascular tissue is visible when the lower stem is cut longitudinally, appearing as a streaking or staining of the xylem vessels. Symptoms are most pronounced during warm days when plants wilt and may partially recover at night. Overall plant stunting, reduced fruit set, and premature defoliation of the lower canopy are common, with the discoloration typically not extending as high up the stem as with Fusarium wilt.

pathogen.verbatim_quote: Verticillium wilt is caused by the soilborne fungi Verticillium dahliae and V. albo-atrum.

visual_symptoms.value: Yellowing and wilting of lower leaves, V-shaped yellow lesions on leaflets, brown vascular discoloration in stem cross-section, asymmetrical symptom development
